lesson.title: Circles Have Rules: Cracking Radius, Circumference, and Arc Length
lesson.summary: Every circle is built from one number, the radius, and that single measurement controls its circumference, area, arcs, and sectors.
lesson.body:
A circle is defined as the set of all points that sit an equal distance, the radius, from a fixed center point. That simple rule is what makes circles so predictable: once you know the radius, you can find everything else about the circle using a small set of formulas. The diameter is just twice the radius (d = 2r), and it is the longest chord you can draw, a chord being any segment connecting two points on the circle.

The circumference, the distance around the circle, is given by C = 2πr (equivalently C = πd). The area enclosed by the circle is A = πr². Both formulas trace back to the same constant, π, which is defined as the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. That ratio is the same for every circle in the universe, tiny or enormous, which is exactly why π shows up in both formulas: circumference scales with the circle's edge, area scales with the circle's interior, and π is the conversion factor that connects a straight-line measurement (the radius) to a curved one.

Arcs and sectors let you work with a slice of the circle instead of the whole thing. A central angle is an angle formed at the center of the circle by two radii, and it tells you what fraction of the full 360 degrees you are looking at. Because the whole circumference corresponds to 360 degrees, an arc's length is that same fraction of the full circumference: arc length = (central angle / 360) × 2πr. Sector area works the same way: sector area = (central angle / 360) × πr². In both cases you are just scaling the whole-circle formula down by the fraction of the circle you are keeping.

Here is a full worked example. Take a circle with radius 6. Its circumference is C = 2π(6) = 12π, which is about 37.70 units. Its area is A = π(6)² = 36π, about 113.10 square units. Now suppose you only want the arc and sector for a 60-degree central angle. Since 60/360 = 1/6, the arc length is (1/6)(12π) = 2π, about 6.28 units, and the sector area is (1/6)(36π) = 6π, about 18.85 square units. Notice the pattern: a 60-degree slice is one-sixth of the circle, so it gets exactly one-sixth of the circumference and one-sixth of the area.

Two more facts are worth knowing cold for the ACT. First, a tangent line touches a circle at exactly one point, and at that point the tangent is always perpendicular to the radius drawn to it, a right angle you can often spot hiding in a diagram. Second, an inscribed angle (formed by two chords meeting on the circle) is always half the central angle that subtends the same arc. Watching for that relationship, along with the radius-tangent right angle, is frequently the fastest route to a correct answer on circle problems that look complicated at first glance.
